name: Camel urine drinking

lead: Camel urine has been used in several traditional medicine systems for centuries, and in parts of the Arabian Peninsula it is still sold in bottles as a remedy. In Yemen it has been used on the scalp, sometimes in the hope of addressing hair loss, which is where it touches on appearance.

Proponents point to old texts and to a hadith about a remedy of camel milk and urine. Laboratory studies have reported effects of camel urine components on some cancer cell lines, while a clinical study in cancer patients reported no benefit.

paras: Traditionally it is drunk, sometimes mixed with camel milk, or applied to the skin and hair. People who use it for hair apply it topically in folk practice; no standard preparation exists.

The World Health Organization has said there is a lack of scientific evidence supporting its medical use and has advised against drinking raw camel milk and urine since MERS-CoV emerged. A clinical study of cancer patients reported two cases of brucellosis. A 2017 study found no virus in the urine of experimentally infected dromedaries.

angle.text: In parts of Yemen camel urine is applied to the scalp in the hope of treating hair loss. This is a traditional belief; no published human study has tested it for hair.

lead: Camel urine drinking is a folk-medicine practice in which the urine of dromedary camels is consumed, or applied to skin and hair, as a remedy. In Yemen it is used both internally and externally, in some cases for hair loss, which is the main way it connects to appearance [1].

Its use draws on several traditions. Ayurvedic texts such as the Caraka-Samhita recommended it for conditions including hiccups, cough and hemorrhoids, and Islamic prophetic medicine cites a hadith describing people who recovered after drinking the milk and urine of a herd of camels. The medieval physician Avicenna also noted a mixture of camel milk and urine for dropsy and jaundice [1].

Research is mostly preclinical. A 2012 study from King Faisal Specialist Hospital reported that components of camel urine were toxic to some human cancer cell lines in the laboratory, while a later study published in a WHO journal found no clinical benefit in cancer patients, with two participants developing brucellosis. The WHO states that scientific evidence supporting medical use is lacking [1].

paras: Camel urine has been used medicinally for centuries. Ayurvedic sources recommended it for several conditions, and others suggested it for inflammation and swelling [1].

In Islamic prophetic medicine the practice rests on a hadith about people who recovered after drinking a herd's milk and urine. Avicenna described a camel milk and urine mixture for dropsy and jaundice [1]. In parts of the Arabian Peninsula bottled camel urine is sold as prophetic medicine [1].

In Yemen camel urine is still drunk and used externally, sometimes for hair loss [1]. Practitioners and users describe it as a traditional scalp remedy; the wiki has found no published trial of it for hair growth.

Preclinical studies have suggested antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, anticancer and cardiovascular effects of camel urine components [1]. A 2012 laboratory study found toxicity toward some human cancer cell lines [1].
A later study in a WHO journal found no clinical benefit in cancer patients and recommended ending promotion of the remedy [1]. The WHO says scientific evidence for medical use is lacking [1].

Two participants in the cancer-patient study developed brucellosis [1]. After the spread of MERS-CoV, the WHO advised against drinking raw camel milk or camel urine or eating undercooked camel meat. A 2017 study found no virus in the urine of experimentally infected dromedaries, suggesting transmission via urine is unlikely [1].
A clinical study in cancer patients reported no clinical benefit and two cases of brucellosis [1]. No studies of camel urine for hair or appearance were found.
